title: Installing a Compiler and Building a Program
summary: Install GCC, Clang or Visual Studio, compile a program split across several files, understand the common compiler flags, and build with CMake.
introduction: You cannot learn C++ without a compiler, and most build problems beginners hit are not C++ problems at all: a missing file on the command line, a wrong flag, or an executable that was never rebuilt. This lesson gets a compiler onto Windows, macOS or Linux, then builds a program split across three files by hand and with CMake, so that the error messages you meet later make sense.
learningObjectives: Install a C++20-capable compiler on your operating system and verify it works
Compile and link a program that spans a header and two source files
Choose the compiler flags that catch bugs early
Build the same program with a minimal CMake project

blocks.text: Three compilers matter in practice and all three support C++20 well: **GCC** (`g++`), **Clang** (`clang++`) and Microsoft's **MSVC** (`cl.exe`). They accept the same language, so the choice depends on your platform. The commands in this tutorial use `g++`; `clang++` takes the same flags.

rows: Visual Studio 2022 Community with the *Desktop development with C++* workload, or MSYS2 and `pacman -S mingw-w64-ucrt-x86_64-gcc`

blocks.text: Verify the install from a terminal. The version line differs by system; what matters is that the command is found and the major version is 13 or newer for GCC, 16 or newer for Clang.

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ --version
g++ (Ubuntu 13.2.0-23ubuntu4) 13.2.0
Copyright (C) 2023 Free Software Foundation, Inc.

blocks.text: Real programs are split into files. A **header** (`.hpp` or `.h`) declares what exists; a **source file** (`.cpp`) defines it; other source files include the header to use it. Declaring in one place and defining in another is what lets the compiler check every call without seeing the function body.

blocks.title: greet.cpp
main.cpp

blocks.text: `#pragma once` stops the header being pasted twice into the same file. Angle brackets (`<string>`) look in the standard library; quotes (`"greet.hpp"`) look next to the current file first. Compile both source files together and the compiler produces one executable.

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra main.cpp greet.cpp -o app
$ ./app
Hello, Ada!
Hello, Linus!

blocks.text: The `-c` flag stops after compiling and writes an object file. Large projects do this so that editing one file only recompiles that file; the final step links the object files together.

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.content:
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -c greet.cpp -o greet.o
$ g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -c main.cpp -o main.o
$ g++ main.o greet.o -o app
$ ./app
Hello, Ada!
Hello, Linus!

rows: Compile as C++20. Use `-std=c++23` for the C++23 examples in this tutorial
Enable the warnings that catch most real bugs (unused variables, missing returns, uninitialised reads)
Warn about compiler extensions that other compilers may reject
Optimise for speed; leave it off while learning so the debugger follows your source
Build with runtime checks that report memory errors and undefined behaviour as they happen (GCC and Clang)
Name the output file; without it you get `a.out` (or `a.exe` on Windows)

blocks.text: On Windows with MSVC, open a *Developer Command Prompt* and the equivalent build is `cl /std:c++20 /EHsc /W4 main.cpp greet.cpp /Fe:app.exe`, then run `app.exe`. MSVC spells C++23 as `/std:c++latest`.

blocks.title: Common mistake: forgetting a source file
blocks.text: Running `g++ -std=c++20 main.cpp -o app` without `greet.cpp` compiles fine but fails at the link stage with a message like `undefined reference to 'greet(std::string const&)'`. The compiler saw the declaration in the header, so it trusted the function exists; only the linker discovers that nobody defined it. The fix is to list every `.cpp` file, never to `#include "greet.cpp"`, which would define the function twice as soon as both files are compiled.

Typing every file on the command line does not scale. **CMake** is the de facto standard build tool for C++: you describe the program once in `CMakeLists.txt` and CMake generates the right build for GCC, Clang or Visual Studio. Install it from cmake.org or your package manager, then put this file next to the three sources.

blocks.title: CMakeLists.txt
blocks.code:
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(greeter CXX)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

add_executable(app main.cpp greet.cpp)

blocks.text: Configure once into a `build` directory, then build. CMake prints its own progress lines (compiler detection, percentages) between the commands shown here; the program's output is what you should compare.

blocks.title: Terminal
blocks.content:
$ cmake -S . -B build
$ cmake --build build
$ ./build/app
Hello, Ada!
Hello, Linus!

blocks.text: `add_executable` lists the sources, `CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD` replaces `-std=c++20`, and `CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF` keeps the code portable. Editors such as VS Code (with the C/C++ and CMake Tools extensions), CLion and Visual Studio all understand this file directly.

blocks.title: Turn warnings on from day one
blocks.text: A warning is a bug the compiler could not quite prove. Treat `-Wall -Wextra` as mandatory and, once your project compiles cleanly, add `-Werror` so that new warnings fail the build instead of scrolling past.

questions.question: You compile `main.cpp` alone, and the build stops with `undefined reference to 'greet(...)'`. Which stage reported the problem?
questions.explanation: An undefined reference is a linker error: compilation succeeded because the header declared the function, but no object file defines it.
options: The operating system when the program starts

questions.question: `#include "greet.hpp"` searches the directory of the current file before the standard library directories.
questions.explanation: Quoted includes look in the including file's directory first; angle-bracket includes go straight to the system and library paths.

seo.title: Installing a C++ Compiler and Building a Program
